claim: THP1 cell line expresses transcripts of all TLRs at significant levels.
source: Lysates from the human myeloid cell line THP1 was used as the source of cellular TLRs, as this line expresses transcripts of all TLRs at significant levels (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating TLR expression levels.

claim: Human SIGLEC-5 and SIGLEC-9 interact with virtually all TLRs tested.
source: Among them, Siglec 5 and 9 cross-reacted with virtually all TLR tested.
evidence: Based on sandwich capture assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Very little interaction was observed between TLRs and human SIGLECS-1, 2, 7, 10 and 11.
source: In contrast, very little interaction was observed between TLRs and SIGLECS-1, 2, 7, 10 and 11.
evidence: Based on sandwich capture assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mouse Siglec-3, E, F and H are broadly cross-reactive with TLRs.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, Siglec-3, E, F and H were broadly cross-reactive, while Siglec-G displayed no interaction with any murine Tlr.
evidence: Based on sandwich capture assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mouse Siglec-G displayed no interaction with any murine TLR.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, Siglec-3, E, F and H were broadly cross-reactive, while Siglec-G displayed no interaction with any murine Tlr.
evidence: Based on sandwich capture assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Siglec-E-Fc, but not control IgG, pulled down Tlr4 in spleen cell lysates.
source: Siglec-E-Fc, but not control IgG, pulled down Tlr4 in the spleen cell lysates (Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on pull-down assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Anti-Siglec-E monoclonal antibodies co-precipitated Tlr4.
source: Anti-Siglec-E monoclonal antibodies co-precipitated Tlr4, while anti-Tlr4 co-precipitated Siglec-E (Figure 1E).
evidence: Based on bi-directional immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Anti-Tlr4 antibodies co-precipitated Siglec-E.
source: Anti-Siglec-E monoclonal antibodies co-precipitated Tlr4, while anti-Tlr4 co-precipitated Siglec-E (Figure 1E).
evidence: Based on bi-directional immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TLR4 directly interacts strongly with human SIGLEC-5, 6, 9, 11 and modestly with SIGLEC-7.
source: The data revealed that TLR4 directly interact strongly with SIGLEC-5, 6, 9, 11 and modestly with SIGLEC-7 (Figure 1F).
evidence: Based on direct binding assay using recombinant TLR4 extracellular domain shown in Figure 1F.

claim: No interaction was observed between human SIGLEC-1, 2, 3, 10 and TLR4.
source: In contrast, no interaction was observed between SIGLEC-1, 2, 3, 10 and TLR4.
evidence: Based on direct binding assay using recombinant TLR4 extracellular domain shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Mouse Siglec-E and F bound strongly to TLR4.
source: Likewise, mouse Siglec-E and F bound strongly to TLR4, with Siglec-3 and H showing modest binding to TLR4, and no binding to TLR4 and Siglec-1, 2 and G (Figure 1G).
evidence: Based on direct binding assay using recombinant TLR4 shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Mouse Siglec-3 and H showed modest binding to TLR4.
source: Likewise, mouse Siglec-E and F bound strongly to TLR4, with Siglec-3 and H showing modest binding to TLR4, and no binding to TLR4 and Siglec-1, 2 and G (Figure 1G).
evidence: Based on direct binding assay using recombinant TLR4 shown in Figure 1G.

claim: No binding was observed between TLR4 and mouse Siglec-1, 2 and G.
source: Likewise, mouse Siglec-E and F bound strongly to TLR4, with Siglec-3 and H showing modest binding to TLR4, and no binding to TLR4 and Siglec-1, 2 and G (Figure 1G).
evidence: Based on direct binding assay using recombinant TLR4 shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Siglec-E contains intracellular immunoreceptor tyrosine inhibitory motif (ITIM) and ITIM-like domains.
source: Since Siglec-E contains intracellular immunoreceptor tyrosine inhibitory motif (ITIM) and ITIM-like domains and associates with molecules known to negatively regulate production of inflammatory cytokines, we compared bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (DC) from WT and Siglece−/− mice for their responses to prototypic TLR ligands.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Siglec-E structure.

claim: Siglec-E associates with molecules known to negatively regulate production of inflammatory cytokines.
source: Since Siglec-E contains intracellular immunoreceptor tyrosine inhibitory motif (ITIM) and ITIM-like domains and associates with molecules known to negatively regulate production of inflammatory cytokines, we compared bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (DC) from WT and Siglece−/− mice for their responses to prototypic TLR ligands.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Siglec-E signaling.

claim: Siglece−/− DC were 1000-fold more responsive to LPS stimulation than Siglece+/+ DC.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, Siglece−/− DC were 1000-fold more responsive to LPS stimulation than Siglece+/+ DC.
evidence: Based on cytokine production data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Siglece−/− DC produced at least 10-fold more cytokines in response to CpG than Siglece+/+ DC.
source: Likewise, Siglece−/− DC produced at least 10-fold more cytokines in response to CpG (Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on cytokine production data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Siglece−/− DC produced significantly more IL-6 in response to TLR1/2, TLR2, TLR3, TLR5, TLR2/6, and TLR8 agonists.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, in addition to an enhanced response to TLR4 and TLR9 ligands, Siglece−/− DC also produced significantly more IL-6 in response to synthetic triacylated lipoprotein Pam3CSK4 (TLR1/2 agonist), heat-killed Listeria monocytogenes (HKLM, Tlr2 agonist), poly(I:C), (TLR3 agonist), Salmonella typhimurium flagellin (ST-FLA, TLR5 agonist), synthetic lipoprotein derived from Mycoplasma salivarium (FSL-1, TLR2/6 agonist) and ssRNA40, a 20-mer phosphorothioate-protected single-stranded RNA oligonucleotide containing a GU-rich sequence (TLR8 agonist).
evidence: Based on cytokine production data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Siglecg−/− and Siglecg+/+ DC exhibited similar responses to all TLR ligands tested except for a modest elevated response to ssRNA40.
source: Except for a modest elevated response to ssRNA40, Siglecg−/− and Siglecg+/+ DC exhibited similar responses to all TLR ligands tested (Figure 2C).
evidence: Based on cytokine production data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Co-precipitation between endogenous TLR4 and Siglec-E was substantially reduced after LPS stimulation.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, co-precipitation between endogenous TLR4 and Siglec-E was substantially reduced after LPS stimulation.
evidence: Based on co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: D2SC cells express Neu1 and to a lesser extent Neu3, but not Neu2 or Neu4.
source: Real-time PCR analysis indicated that D2SC cells express Neu1 and to a lesser extent Neu3, but not Neu2 or Neu4 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LPS stimulation led to robust translocation of Neu1 to cell surface where it co-localized with TLR4.
source: Fluorescent microscopy revealed a robust translocation of Neu1 to cell surface where it co-localized with TLR4 (Figure 3C), which is similar to a previous report on macrophages (Liang et al., 2006).
evidence: Based on fluorescent microscopy data shown in Figure 3C and comparison to published literature.

claim: Flow cytometry confirmed a time-dependent translocation of Neu1 between 6–18 hr following LPS stimulation.
source: Flow cytometry confirmed a time-dependent translocation of Neu1 between 6–18 hr following LPS stimulation (Figure 3D).
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A specific Neu1-TLR4 association was observed only after LPS stimulation.
source: As shown in Figure 3E, a specific Neu1-TLR4 association was observed only after LPS stimulation.
evidence: Based on co-immunoprecipitation data after cross-linking shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Silencing of Neu1 increased binding of Siglec-E-Fc to DC.
source: As shown in Figure 3F, silencing of Neu1 increased binding of Siglec-E-Fc to DC.
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: shRNA silencing of Neu1 abrogated the LPS-induced disassociation of Siglec-E-TLR4 complexes.
source: As shown in Figure 3G, shRNA silencing of Neu1 abrogated the LPS-induced disassociation of Siglec-E-TLR4 complexes.
evidence: Based on co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: shRNA silencing of Neu3 had no effect on Siglec-E-TLR4 interaction.
source: In contrast, shRNA silencing of Neu3 had no effect on Siglec-E-TLR4 interaction.
evidence: Based on co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: LPS-induced cytokine production was more significantly reduced by Neu1 shRNAs Sh1 and Sh2 than by Sh3.
source: Corresponding with the silencing efficiencies, LPS-induced cytokine production was more significantly reduced by Sh1 and Sh2 than by Sh3, which had partial effect when compared to scramble control (Figure 3I).
evidence: Based on cytokine production data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: LPS stimulation led to upregulation of cell surface Neu1 on DCs, macrophages, and neutrophils.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, LPS stimulation led to upregulation of cell surface Neu1 on DCs, macrophages, and neutrophils.
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data from in vivo LPS-treated mice shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Siglec-E-Fc showed reduced binding to DCs after LPS stimulation, and this effect was rescued by incubation with a sialidase inhibitor.
source: Correspondingly, Siglec-E-Fc showed reduced binding to DCs after LPS stimulation, and this effect was rescued by incubation with a sialidase inhibitor, indicating that Siglec-E binding to its ligands was disrupted by sialidase activity (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Bone marrow from CD45.2+ Neu1−/− donors was as competent as WT bone marrow in reconstituting lethally irradiated CD45.1 hosts.
source: Bone marrow from CD45.2+ Neu1−/− donors was as competent as WT bone marrow in reconstituting lethally irradiated CD45.1 hosts (Figure 4C), and the major hematopoietic cellular components were not affected by Neu1 deficiency (Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data from bone marrow chimeric mice shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: The major hematopoietic cellular components were not affected by Neu1 deficiency.
source: Bone marrow from CD45.2+ Neu1−/− donors was as competent as WT bone marrow in reconstituting lethally irradiated CD45.1 hosts (Figure 4C), and the major hematopoietic cellular components were not affected by Neu1 deficiency (Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data from bone marrow chimeric mice shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Animals reconstituted with Neu1−/− bone marrow had increased sialylation and Siglec-E binding to DC.
source: Animals reconstituted with Neu1−/− bone marrow had increased sialylation and Siglec-E binding to DC (Figure 4E), and more specifically, Siglec-E-TLR4 association (Figure 4F).
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Animals reconstituted with Neu1−/− bone marrow had increased Siglec-E-TLR4 association.
source: Animals reconstituted with Neu1−/− bone marrow had increased sialylation and Siglec-E binding to DC (Figure 4E), and more specifically, Siglec-E-TLR4 association (Figure 4F).
evidence: Based on capture assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: 100% of mice reconstituted with WT bone marrow cells succumbed to all doses of LPS tested (100-400 μg).
source: As shown in Figure 4G, 100% of mice reconstituted with WT bone marrow cells succumbed to all doses of LPS tested.
evidence: Based on survival data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The majority of mice reconstituted with Neu1−/− bone marrow were resistant to 100 and 200 μg doses of LPS.
source: In contrast, the majority of mice reconstituted with Neu1−/− bone marrow were resistant to 100 and 200 μg doses of LPS.
evidence: Based on survival data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Neu1−/− >WT chimera mice produced significantly less IL-6 and TNFα following LPS stimulation.
source: Corresponding with the increased resistance, the Neu1−/− >WT chimera mice produced significantly less IL-6 and TNFα following LPs stimulation (Figure 4H).
evidence: Based on cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: All mice that received sialidase inhibitors (Neu5Ac2en and Neu5Gc2en) survived LPS challenge, while 80% of vehicle-treated mice succumbed.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, while 80% of the vehicle-treated mice succumbed to LPS challenge, all mice that received the inhibitors survived throughout the observation period.
evidence: Based on survival data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Sialidase inhibitors had no significant effect on the first cytokine storm, but drastically inhibited IL-6 and TNF-α production 24 and 48 hr post LPS administration.
source: Interestingly, the inhibitors had no significant effect on the first cytokine storm, but drastically inhibited IL-6 and TNF-α production 24 and 48 hr post LPS administration (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Based on cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Neu5Gc2en accounted for most, if not all, of the therapeutic effect of the sialidase inhibitor mixture.
source: Of the two inhibitors used, Neu5Gc2en accounted for most, if not all, of the therapeutic effect (Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on survival data comparing individual inhibitors shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Neu5Gc2en conferred complete protection when administered 6 hr after LPS injection.
source: Indeed, as shown in Figure 5E, Neu5Gc2en conferred complete protection even when it was administered 6 hr after LPS injection.
evidence: Based on survival data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Neu5Gc2en protected mice against lethal E. coli (strain 25922) infection.
source: As shown in Figure 5F, Neu5Gc2en protected mice against lethal E. coli (strain 25922) infection.
evidence: Based on survival data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: LPS treatment reduced both Siglec-E:Tlr4 and Siglec-F:Tlr4 interactions.
source: As shown in Figure 5G, LPS treatment reduced both Siglec-E:Tlr4 and Siglec-F:Tlr4 interactions, while treatment with Neu5Gc2en preserved both interactions.
evidence: Based on in vitro capture assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Treatment with Neu5Gc2en preserved both Siglec-E:Tlr4 and Siglec-F:Tlr4 interactions.
source: As shown in Figure 5G, LPS treatment reduced both Siglec-E:Tlr4 and Siglec-F:Tlr4 interactions, while treatment with Neu5Gc2en preserved both interactions.
evidence: Based on in vitro capture assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Both Neu1 and Neu2 were efficiently inhibited by Neu5Ac2en and Neu5Gc2en.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, while both Neu1 and Neu2 were efficiently inhibited by Neu5Ac2en and Neu5Gc2en, Neu3 and Neu4 are largely resistant.
evidence: Based on sialidase activity assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Neu3 and Neu4 are largely resistant to Neu5Ac2en and Neu5Gc2en.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, while both Neu1 and Neu2 were efficiently inhibited by Neu5Ac2en and Neu5Gc2en, Neu3 and Neu4 are largely resistant.
evidence: Based on sialidase activity assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Neu1 was 10-fold more sensitive to Neu5Gc2en than to Neu5Ac2en.
source: Importantly, while Neu2 was equally sensitive to both inhibitors, Neu1 was 10-fold more sensitive to Neu5Gc2en than to Neu5Ac2en.
evidence: Based on sialidase activity assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Neu2 was equally sensitive to both Neu5Ac2en and Neu5Gc2en.
source: Importantly, while Neu2 was equally sensitive to both inhibitors, Neu1 was 10-fold more sensitive to Neu5Gc2en than to Neu5Ac2en.
evidence: Based on sialidase activity assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Targeted mutation of Neu1 reduced production of both IL-6 and TNFα by more than 70%.
source: As shown in Figure 6B, targeted mutation of Neu1 reduced production of both IL-6 and TNFα by more than 70%.
evidence: Based on cytokine production data from Neu1−/− DC shown in Figure 6B.

claim: WT DC responded to Neu5Gc2en inhibition, while Neu1−/− DC were largely resistant.
source: Importantly, while WT DC responded to Neu5Gc2en inhibition, Neu1−/− DC were largely resistant, confirming that Neu5Gc2en inhibits cytokine responses by targeting Neu1.
evidence: Based on cytokine production data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Neu5Gc2en was therapeutic only in WT, but not Neu1−/− chimeric mice challenged with lethal LPS.
source: As shown in Figure 6C,D, Neu5Gc2en was therapeutic only in WT, but not Neu1−/− chimeric mice.
evidence: Based on survival data from bone marrow chimeric mice shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: All sialidase activity in D2SC cells was eliminated by shRNA silencing of Neu1.
source: Regardless of LPS stimulation, all sialidase activity was eliminated by shRNA silencing of Neu1, which indicated that this assay measured primarily Neu1 activity in the D2SC cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: Based on sialidase activity assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Upon LPS stimulation, the total Neu1 activity was increased, and all activity was inhibited by Neu5Gc2en.
source: Upon LPS stimulation, the total Neu1 activity was increased, and all activity was inhibited by Neu5Gc2en (Figure 7A).
evidence: Based on sialidase activity assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A depot of Neu1 resistant to extracellularly-administered Neu5Gc2en was present in unstimulated D2SC cells.
source: In contrast to LPS-stimulated D2SC, a depot of Neu1 resistant to extracellularly-administered Neu5Gc2en was present in the unstimulated D2SC.
evidence: Based on sialidase activity assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The plasma membrane sialidase activity was significantly reduced by Neu5Gc2en, while the cytoplasmic sialidase activity was unaffected.
source: As shown in Figure 7B, while the plasma membrane sialidase activity was significantly reduced, the cytoplasmic sialidase activity was unaffected.
evidence: Based on sialidase activity assay of fractionated cell components shown in Figure 7B.

claim: TLR4 is a cell surface glycoprotein.
source: Since TLR4 is a cell surface glycoprotein while Neu1 is primarily lysosomal, we evaluated whether Neu1 translocates to the cell surface following LPS stimulation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of TLR4 localization.

claim: Neu1 is primarily lysosomal.
source: Since TLR4 is a cell surface glycoprotein while Neu1 is primarily lysosomal, we evaluated whether Neu1 translocates to the cell surface following LPS stimulation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Neu1 localization.

claim: TLRs sense a variety of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), ranging from microbial glycan, bacterial glycolipids, flagellin, and viral and bacterial nucleic acids.
source: Over the following decades, TLRs have emerged as a family of PRRs that sense a variety of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), ranging from microbial glycan, bacterial glycolipids, flagellin, and viral and bacterial nucleic acids (Kawai and Akira, 2010).
evidence: Based on citation to review by Kawai and Akira.

claim: TLRs sense cellular components released after cellular injuries, such as heat-shock proteins, HMGB1, and S100.
source: Surprisingly, accumulating data demonstrated that TLRs also sense cellular components released after cellular injuries, such as heat-shock proteins (Millar et al., 2003), HMGB1 (Apetoh et al., 2007; Ivanov et al., 2007; Tian et al., 2007) and S100 (Hiratsuka et al., 2008; Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on citations to multiple studies.

claim: CD24-Siglec-G/10 interactions selectively inhibit host responses to DAMPs without affecting responses to PAMPs.
source: We have reported that CD24-Siglec-G/10 interactions selectively inhibit host responses to DAMPs without affecting responses to PAMPs (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Most Siglecs have intracellular domains capable of inhibitory signaling.
source: Most Siglecs have intracellular domains capable of inhibitory signaling.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Siglec structure and function.

claim: CD24-Siglec-G interactions are disrupted by bacterial sialidase and such disruptions exacerbate sepsis.
source: Our previous studies have demonstrated that CD24-Siglec-G interactions are disrupted by bacterial sialidase and that such disruptions exacerbates sepsis (Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Mammals express at least four sialidases, Neu1-4.
source: On the other hand, mammals express at least four sialidases, Neu1-4 (Miyagi and Yamaguchi, 2012).
evidence: Based on citation to review by Miyagi and Yamaguchi.

claim: Activation of TLR can be attenuated by sialidase inhibitors.
source: Several studies have suggested that activation of TLR can be attenuated by sialidase inhibitors (Amith et al., 2010; Abdulkhalek et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on citations to studies by Amith et al. and Abdulkhalek et al.

claim: Both Neu1 and Neu3 have been suggested as targets of sialidase inhibitors.
source: Both Neu1 and Neu3 have been suggested as targets of the inhibitors (Amith et al., 2010; Abdulkhalek et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on citations to studies by Amith et al. and Abdulkhalek et al.

claim: Neu1 has been shown to cause TLR4 dimerization, which was suggested to be important for its regulation of TLR4 activation.
source: Neu1 has been shown to cause TLR4 dimerization, which was suggested to be important for its regulation of TLR4 activation (Amith et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on citation to study by Amith et al.

claim: Siglece deletion enhanced dendritic cell responses to all microbial TLR ligands tested.
source: Correspondingly, Siglece deletion enhanced dendritic cell responses to all microbial TLR ligands tested, while Siglecg deletion did not affect the responses to these ligands.
evidence: Based on cytokine production data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Siglecg deletion did not affect dendritic cell responses to microbial TLR ligands.
source: Correspondingly, Siglece deletion enhanced dendritic cell responses to all microbial TLR ligands tested, while Siglecg deletion did not affect the responses to these ligands.
evidence: Based on cytokine production data shown in Figure 2.

claim: TLR4 activation triggers Neu1 translocation to cell surface to disrupt TLR4:Siglec-E interaction.
source: TLR4 activation triggers Neu1 translocation to cell surface to disrupt TLR4:Siglec-E interaction.
evidence: Based on fluorescence microscopy, flow cytometry, and co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Sialidase inhibitor Neu5Gc2en prevented TLR4 ligand-induced disruption of TLR4:Siglec E/F interactions.
source: Conversely, sialidase inhibitor Neu5Gc2en prevented TLR4 ligand-induced disruption of TLR4:Siglec E/F interactions.
evidence: Based on capture assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Absence of Neu1 in hematopoietic cells protected mice against endotoxemia.
source: Absence of Neu1 in hematopoietic cells or systematic treatment with sialidase inhibitor Neu5Gc2en protected mice against endotoxemia.
evidence: Based on survival data from bone marrow chimeric mice shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Systematic treatment with sialidase inhibitor Neu5Gc2en protected mice against endotoxemia.
source: Absence of Neu1 in hematopoietic cells or systematic treatment with sialidase inhibitor Neu5Gc2en protected mice against endotoxemia.
evidence: Based on survival data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Neu5Gc2en protects mice against endotoxemia by targeting Neu1.
source: Therefore, Neu5Gc2en protects mice against endotoxemia by targeting Neu1.
evidence: Based on survival data from Neu1−/− chimeric mice treated with Neu5Gc2en shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Neu5Gc2en selectively inhibits cell surface Neu1.
source: Since Neu5Gc2en selectively inhibited cell surface Neu1, it is possible to preserve intracellular Neu1 function while targeting cell surface Neu1 with Neu5Gc2en.
evidence: Based on sialidase activity assay of fractionated cell components shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Functional redundancy of Siglec-E and Siglec-F explains lack of strong phenotype of mice with Siglec-E deletion in endotoxemia.
source: Functional redundancy of the two Siglecs explains lack of strong phenotype of mice with Siglec-E deletion in endotoxemia (data not shown).
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that both Siglec-E and Siglec-F interact with TLR4.

claim: Mice with homozygous deletion of the Neu1 locus develop clinical abnormalities reminiscent of early-onset sialidosis in children.
source: However, mice with homozygous deletion of the Neu1 locus develop clinical abnormalities reminiscent of early-onset sialidosis in children, including severe nephropathy, progressive edema, splenomegaly, kyphosis and urinary excretion of sialylated oligosaccharides (de Geest et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on citation to study by de Geest et al.

claim: Neu3 is a constitutive cell surface sialidase.
source: As a control, we also tested the impact of silencing Neu3, which is a constitutive cell surface sialidase.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Neu3 localization.

claim: Neu1 translocation during differentiation from monocytes to macrophage occurs by a route used by MHC class II.
source: The molecular mechanism for TLR4-induced Neu1 translocation is largely unclear, although Neu1 translocation during differentiation from monocytes to macrophage occurs by a route used by MHC class II (Liang et al., 2006).
evidence: Based on citation to study by Liang et al.

claim: Engagement of TLR4 activates cell surface Neu1 activity, perhaps by G protein-coupled receptor and matrix metalloproteinase-9-dependent mechanisms.
source: Engagement of TLR4 also activates cell surface Neu1 activity, perhaps by G protein-coupled receptor and matrix metalloproteinase-9-dependent mechanisms (Amith et al., 2009; Abdulkhalek et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on citations to studies by Amith et al. and Abdulkhalek et al.

claim: TLR-mediated trans-regulation of cellular glycosylation was described through genetic screen in Drosophila.
source: It is also of interest to note that TLR-mediated trans-regulation of cellular glycosylation was described through genetic screen in Drosophila (Seppo et al., 2003), although the functional significance was not clear.
evidence: Based on citation to study by Seppo et al.

claim: CD33-like Siglecs are known to be readily endocytosed.
source: As a member of CD33-like Siglecs that are known to be readily endocytosed (Walter et al., 2008), Siglec-E may form physical complexes with endosomal TLRs.
evidence: Based on citation to study by Walter et al.

claim: Siglec-E may form physical complexes with endosomal TLRs.
source: As a member of CD33-like Siglecs that are known to be readily endocytosed (Walter et al., 2008), Siglec-E may form physical complexes with endosomal TLRs.
evidence: Based on inference from Siglec-E's ability to be endocytosed and its effect on endosomal TLRs.

claim: Sepsis remains a major challenge despite advances in antibiotics.
source: Sepsis remains a major challenge despite advances in antibiotics, and many sepsis cases are caused by gram-negative bacteria (Hurley, 1995; Angus et al., 2001; Seyrantepe et al., 2003; Dombrovskiy et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on citations to multiple studies.

claim: Many sepsis cases are caused by gram-negative bacteria.
source: Sepsis remains a major challenge despite advances in antibiotics, and many sepsis cases are caused by gram-negative bacteria (Hurley, 1995; Angus et al., 2001; Seyrantepe et al., 2003; Dombrovskiy et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on citations to multiple studies.

claim: Most pathogens do not encode sialidase.
source: However, most pathogens do not encode sialidase.
evidence: Based on general knowledge of pathogen biology.

claim: Mutation of Neu1 causes sialidosis.
source: However, since mutation of Neu1 cause sialidosis (Seyrantepe et al., 2003), it is of interest to consider how potential side-effects associated with Neu1 inactivation may be avoided.
evidence: Based on citation to study by Seyrantepe et al.

claim: An effective sialidase inhibitor can confer protection by selectively targeting cell surface Neu1.
source: Fortunately, our data demonstrate that an effective sialidase inhibitor can confer protection by selectively targeting cell surface Neu1, perhaps by virtue of poor drug accessibility to the intracellular compartment.
evidence: Based on sialidase activity assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: It is feasible to target Neu1 therapeutically without side effects associated with disruption of the intracellular sialidase activity.
source: Therefore, it is feasible to target Neu1 therapeutically without side effects associated with disruption of the intracellular sialidase activity, the known cause of sialidosis.
evidence: Based on inference from the selective inhibition of cell surface Neu1 by Neu5Gc2en.

claim: The data establish a missing link between the TLR and Siglec families of pattern recognition receptors.
source: Taken together, our data establish a missing link between the TLR and Siglec families of pattern recognition receptors.
evidence: Based on the extensive interaction data between TLRs and Siglecs shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: The specificity of individual Siglecs allows them to play distinct roles in innate immunity.
source: The specificity of individual Siglecs allow them to play distinct roles in innate immunity, while regulation of the interaction by host sialidase suggest a novel approach for treatment of inflammatory diseases, such as sepsis.
evidence: Based on the differential binding patterns and functional effects of different Siglecs shown in the manuscript.

claim: Regulation of Siglec-TLR interaction by host sialidase suggests a novel approach for treatment of inflammatory diseases, such as sepsis.
source: The specificity of individual Siglecs allow them to play distinct roles in innate immunity, while regulation of the interaction by host sialidase suggest a novel approach for treatment of inflammatory diseases, such as sepsis.
evidence: Based on the therapeutic effect of Neu1 inhibition shown in the manuscript.

claim: Infection can boost inflammation through microbial sialidase or by inducing translocation of host Neu1 to the cell surface to disarm the Siglec-mediated negative regulation of TLR function.
source: Infection can boost inflammation through microbial sialidase, as we have recently reported (Chen et al., 2011), or as shown herein, by inducing translocation of host Neu1 to the cell surface to disarm the Siglec-mediated negative regulation of TLR function.
evidence: Based on data showing Neu1 translocation and disruption of Siglec-TLR interaction after LPS stimulation.

claim: A positive feedback is created to release the Siglec brake for TLR activation through Neu1 translocation induced by microbial TLR ligand.
source: Since the Neu1 translocation is induced by microbial TLR ligand, a positive feedback is created to release the Siglec brake for TLR activation.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that TLR activation induces Neu1 translocation which disrupts Siglec-TLR interaction.

claim: Under steady-state conditions, TLR-induced inflammation may be relatively moderate as TLR functions are restrained by sialoside-based pattern recognition.
source: By virtue of the broad and direct interaction between TLRs and Siglecs, one may envision that under steady-state conditions, TLR-induced inflammation may be relatively moderate as TLR functions are either directly (in case of Siglec-E) or indirectly (in case of Siglec-G) restrained by sialoside-based pattern recognition.
evidence: Based on inference from the inhibitory effect of Siglecs on TLR function.

claim: In case of tissue injury, a moderate inflammation may be beneficial for tissue remodeling and regeneration.
source: In case of tissue injury, a moderate inflammation may be beneficial for tissue remodeling and regeneration (Takahashi et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on citation to study by Takahashi et al.

claim: Siglecs constitute the first class of cell surface pattern recognition receptors that are directly involved in regulation of TLR function.
source: Although a number of intracellular negative regulators have been described to regulate TLR function (Kawai and Akira, 2010), to our knowledge, Siglecs constitute the first class of cell surface pattern recognition receptors that are directly involved in regulation of TLR function.
evidence: Based on comparison to known intracellular regulators and the novel finding of direct Siglec-TLR interaction.

claim: Blocking specific Siglecs is unlikely to significantly impact the susceptibility to endotoxemia because one Siglec can interact with multiple TLRs, and each TLR with multiple Siglecs.
source: However, since one Siglec can interact with multiple TLRs, and each TLR with multiple Siglecs, it is unlikely that blocking specific Siglecs may significantly impact the susceptibility to endotoxemia.
evidence: Based on inference from the promiscuous binding patterns observed.

claim: Targeting host sialidase may be more effective than blocking specific Siglecs because sialidases may regulate multiple Siglec-TLR interactions.
source: In contrast, as sialidases may regulate multiple Siglec-TLR interactions, targeting host sialidase may be more effective.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that Neu1 regulates multiple Siglec-TLR interactions.

claim: Neu1 may serve as a new therapeutic target for endotoxic shock.
source: Therefore, Neu1 may serve as a new therapeutic target for endotoxic shock.
evidence: Based on the protective effect of Neu1 inhibition shown in the manuscript.

claim: Endogenous sialidases may be easier to target than bacterial and viral sialidases as they are both limited in diversity and unlikely to acquire drug resistance through mutation.
source: Unlike bacterial and viral sialidases, endogenous sialidases may be easier to target as they are both limited in diversity and unlikely to acquire drug resistance through mutation.
evidence: Based on inference from the biological properties of host vs. microbial enzymes.

claim: The Siglec family of PRR may help the innate immune system to discriminate between infection and tissue injury by two distinct mechanisms.
source: The Siglec family of PRR may help the innate immune system to discriminate between infection and tissue injury by two distinct mechanisms.
evidence: Based on the differential mechanisms of Siglec-G and Siglec-E described in the manuscript.

claim: Siglec-G/10 selectively represses inflammation by binding to a DAMPs-associated natural ligand, such as CD24, to inhibit host response to DAMPs.
source: First, as represented by Siglec-G/10, which does not directly associate with TLR, Siglecs may selective repress inflammation by binding to a DAMPs-associated natural ligand, such as CD24, to inhibit host response to DAMPs.
evidence: Based on previous findings cited in the manuscript.

claim: Siglec-E regulates inflammation to endogenous TLR ligands by default through direct association with TLR.
source: Second, as represented by Siglec-E which directly associates with TLR, Siglecs may regulate inflammation to endogenous TLR ligands by default.
evidence: Based on the direct interaction data and functional studies shown in the manuscript.

claim: Infection can exacerbate inflammatory cytokine production by inducing translocation of intracellular sialidase or by producing microbial sialidases to disrupt direct Siglec-TLR interactions.
source: By either inducing translocation of intracellular sialidase or by producing microbial sialidases, infection can exacerbate inflammatory cytokine production to disrupt direct Siglec-TLR interactions (Figure 8).
evidence: Based on the data showing Neu1 translocation and disruption of Siglec-TLR interaction.
